Hiring in-house takes 60–90 days. But what if your project only lasts 2.5 months?  

That was the exact challenge a German automotive client faced recently.  They urgently needed a specialized Scala developer for a 2.5-month sprint. 

In Germany, the standard legal notice period (Kündigungsfrist) is 3 months. In other words: the notice period was literally longer than the entire project scope.  

Instead of burning months and budget on internal recruiting, we matched and deployed a vetted senior engineer in under 60 hours.  

In this video, I break down when Staff Augmentation beats in-house hiring (and when it doesn’t):  
💡 Key takeaways: 
1️⃣ The 2–6 Month Dilemma: Why top senior talent rejects short-term full-time contracts, and why hiring full-time for sprints creates severance overhead. 
2️⃣ The 4-in-1 Stack (Case Study): How we staffed a rare hybrid engineer (Flutter + AR + AI + IoT) with a 24/7 on-call SLA. 
3️⃣ The 80% Rule: Why 80% of candidates on the market fail the "Triple-Fit" (Product, Culture, and Tech depth). 

🎥 Watch the full breakdown in the video below!  

💬 What’s your biggest bottleneck right now: finding niche talent or time-to-hire?

Graduate jobs have fallen 85% since 2017. Everyone is blaming AI. 
Everyone is wrong.

Over a million 16 to 24 year olds are NEET for the first time since 2013. Youth unemployment is 16.2%, an 11-year high. And there are 7.45 million people aged 16 to 24 in this country, the most since records began in 1992.

The biggest cohort of young people in a generation is arriving at the smallest front door in a generation.

The lazy explanation is AI. ChatGPT ate the graduate scheme.

Except when Deloitte asked Britain's finance directors why they'd stopped hiring graduates, the answer wasn't AI. It was cost control. AI is the story boards tell the press. The spreadsheet tells a different one.

So let's look at the spreadsheet.

In 1999 Tony Blair set a target: half of all young people into university. We hit it in 2019. We built a machine that doubles the supply of graduates and told them the degree was the ticket. Education, education, education.

Then, over the same 25 years, we did this to the ticket collector:

① Cut the employer NI threshold to £5,000, so the cheapest hire in the building became proportionally the most expensive to employ.

② Pushed the minimum wage for 21 year olds to two thirds of median earnings, closing the gap between "trainee" and "experienced".

③ Loaded day-one rights, guaranteed hours and tribunal exposure onto the first contract an employer offers a 22 year old with no track record.

Every one of those may be defensible on its own. Together they have abolished the office apprenticeship. The junior role was never really a job. It was a paid education the employer funded because it was cheap. It isn't cheap any more, so it doesn't exist.

The last two times youth unemployment sat above 20%, in 1984 and 2011, the research afterwards was brutal. People who start their careers in a slump earn less for a decade. Not because they're worse. Because the first rung was missing and they never quite catch up.
We are building that cohort right now, on purpose, with a policy stack designed by people who all got their first job when the rung was still there.

For those of us in and around recruitment this is not somebody else's problem. Our industry is one of the last that still hires raw 22 year olds in volume and trains them on the phone. Trainee consultant desks are the graduate scheme that never got a press release. If the economics of the first job are broken, they're broken for us too.

So here's the argument. Stop blaming the robots. The entry-level job wasn't automated. It was priced out. And a government that wants to fix youth unemployment needs to make the first hire the cheapest one in the building again, not the riskiest.

The Finance Talent Gap Nobody Saw Coming (And How Firms Are Solving It)

There's a quiet problem sitting inside most finance and accounting teams right now. There simply aren't enough skilled people to go around, and it's no longer just a feeling leaders have. A recent Controllers Council study found that 61% of finance leaders are already dealing with some level of talent shortage in their teams, and in many organizations it's now taking two months or longer just to fill a single open accounting role.

Part of the reason is retirement. A large share of experienced CPAs are approaching the end of their careers, and fewer graduates are choosing accounting to replace them. Meanwhile, the job itself is changing quickly, thanks to AI, automation, and rising reporting standards. So even the talent that is available often doesn't have the exact skills firms need today.

Instead of waiting for this gap to close on its own, firms are responding in two smart ways.
The first is contract and flexible talent. Rather than hiring full time for every role, more companies are bringing in contract professionals for specific projects, busy seasons, or specialized skills they don't need year round. This gives firms the expertise they need, without the long hiring cycles or the risk of overstaffing when things slow down. It also gives finance professionals more flexibility in how and where they work, which is exactly what a lot of talent wants today.

The second is upskilling. Firms are investing more in training their existing teams, especially in areas like data analysis, AI tools, forecasting, and reporting. It's no longer enough for finance professionals to just be good with numbers. They also need to be comfortable with technology and able to turn data into decisions.

At the same time, all of this is landing on one desk more than any other, the CFO's. The role has expanded well beyond budgets and financial statements. Today's CFOs are expected to guide technology decisions, manage risk, support hiring strategy, and act as a strategic partner to the CEO, not just report on what already happened.

So what does this mean if you're in finance or leading a team right now? It means flexibility and continuous learning aren't optional extras anymore, they are the new baseline. The professionals and firms who adapt early, whether that means picking up a new skill, embracing contract work, or rethinking how their finance function operates, will be the ones best positioned for what comes next.

The talent shortage isn't going away soon. But firms that treat it as a chance to build smarter, leaner, more skilled teams will come out ahead.
Is your team leaning more toward upskilling, contract talent, or both? Would love to hear how you're navigating it.

A few years ago, most conversations were about getting hired, getting promoted, and growing fast.
Today, it’s a little different.

AI replacing or changing certain tasks.
Companies hiring for skills that didn’t even exist a few years ago.

Candidates wondering whether their current skills will still be relevant two years from now.

Companies want the right people but they’re also thinking harder about which roles they really need.

Candidates want jobs but they’re also asking a bigger question:
Where should I invest my time and skills?

Technology is going to keep changing the way we work. Hiring will change with it. Some roles will disappear, new ones will emerge, and many existing roles will simply evolve.
The people who keep learning, adapting and staying curious will have an important advantage.

💰 Is the current economic climate changing the way companies are approaching SAP S/4HANA projects?

I'm seeing more conversations around cost, project duration, headcount and consultant utilisation and I'm interested to hear whether others are seeing the same.
SAP S/4HANA transformation isn't disappearing. In fact, SAP continues to report strong cloud growth, while companies are still progressing with major transformation programmes.

But the way companies are delivering these projects appears to be changing.
A few things I'm hearing more often:

🔹 Project budgets are under greater scrutiny
Clients want to understand exactly where their external spend is going and what value each consultant is bringing.

🔹 Long-term projects are being challenged
Rather than committing to large teams for extended periods, companies are looking for more targeted expertise at specific stages of the programme.

🔹 Headcount freezes are affecting project teams
Some organisations are holding permanent hiring while continuing critical transformation work through existing teams and contractors.

🔹 The demand for specialists remains
Business Partner, FICO, SD, MM, EWM, BW/4HANA, BTP, Data Migration and other specialist skills can still be critical — but clients increasingly need the right specialist at the right point in the project.

🔹 AI is changing the conversation 🤖
SAP itself is highlighting the potential for AI to reduce the time and cost involved in S/4HANA transformation activities.

And this raises an interesting question for both SAP clients and consultants:
👇 What are you seeing in the market?

For SAP Clients / Hiring Managers:
Are economic pressures causing you to:
1️⃣ Delay projects
2️⃣ Reduce project teams

4️⃣ Shorten contract durations
5️⃣ Demand more specialised consultants
6️⃣ Look at AI/automation to reduce project costs
7️⃣ No major change, projects are continuing as planned

🔹 More competition for roles?

Several worrying trends are converging at once. At the top of the income ladder, AI is taking a swing at jobs. In the middle, standard robotics and now humanoids are taking over repetitive but still higher-value work, because it makes ROI work.

What's left are low value-add jobs that don't pay the bills…

The standard story is that millennials and Gen Z won't do the work. The numbers say something else: they won't do work that mathematically cannot produce an adult life.
In the US, 18 of the 25 most common occupations pay below the wage needed to rent a modest two-bedroom. Those 18 occupations employ roughly 74 million people. In the EU, the average age of leaving the parental home is 26. In Slovakia, it's 31.

The usual answer is "start low, work up." Studies show that the ladder is disappearing. About 90% of Americans born in 1940 out-earned their parents. For those born in the 1980s, it's roughly 50%. Today, 42% of recent US graduates work in jobs that don't require a degree and don't outearn their parents.

Now the part almost nobody has priced in.

Every previous wave of automation went bottom-up. Machines took the dangerous and physically punishing work first, and the reward was climbing into cognitive work. AI runs that escalator backward. The most AI-exposed occupations pay 47% MORE than the least exposed. Employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in exposed roles sits 19% below trend — not through firing, but through simply not hiring.

So why doesn't robotics clear out the bottom?

Because robot business cases are priced against the wage they replace. A humanoid runs an effective $9-10/hour against a loaded warehouse worker at $22-45. Below roughly $12-15/hour, the payback never closes. Moravec's paradox does the rest: a machine can draft a contract long before it can dress a frail person.

The result is an anti-selection on job quality. The better the job, the sooner the machine arrives. The worse the job, the longer it stays human.

Work that is too cheap to automate, and too poor to live on. Low pay has become a job's best protection.

BLS says the five occupations adding the most US jobs by 2034 are home health aides, stockers, fast food workers, cooks, and software developers. Four of the five sit below the rent line.

To underscore the point, this picture, the research, and my reasoning were made with AI, not a designer... And that is exactly the conundrum. Statistics already show how society is eroding, but for us fortunate few, it's a positive game-changer...

I followed Andon Labs' vending machine experiment closely, the one where the AI shopkeeper kept handing out discounts and stocking tungsten cubes. Somehow I missed the sequel. This spring they gave an AI agent a real café in Stockholm.

The agent is called Mona. Human baristas make the coffee, and Mona runs the rest: hiring, suppliers, permits, pricing.

It reads like a new manager's first week. She ordered 120 eggs for a kitchen with no stove, and 6,000 napkins. She bought 1,331 bakery items and sold 326. By the end of June the café made about $9,000 and spent $38,000.

Then Andon switched models. Gemini was too generous. One customer talked it into dropping an espresso from $3.60 to $1. GPT-5.5 was much tougher on price but swung the other way on stock, and some days it skipped the bakery order on purpose until the shelves were empty. Neither made the café profitable, and neither acted on easy ways to grow sales, like opening earlier.

Two different models, similar result. But I don't think the model was ever the problem. What was missing was an operating layer around it.

Anyone who has run a retail shop knows what Mona was missing. We built it decades ago for new managers. Par levels, order guides, delivery cut-offs, limits on who can discount what, someone to call when things go sideways. We never hand a new store manager unlimited judgment. We give them a system where the right call is the easy one.

What also deserves attention is how Mona cut corners. She signed a three-year electricity contract without comparing suppliers, because that provider didn't need a human ID check. That is not stupid. It's what an agent does when all it cares about is getting the task done.

In a store network, that looks like the skipped approval, the missed food-safety step, or the supplier picked because onboarding was quickest. A smarter model won't fix that. You need guardrails before go-live: spend limits, a required quote comparison, and a human sign-off on anything that commits you beyond a week.

Every retail and QSR leader rolling out agents will have to choose: upgrade the model, or build the operating layer around it. Only one shows up on your P&L.

One last detail. Mona messaged the baristas at midnight and sometimes asked them to buy supplies on their personal credit cards. So, it isn't ready to run a store. It has definitely met a few bosses, though.

Two findings this month seem to contradict each other on AI interviews.

Bullhorn (~2,300 candidates): 
92% of those interviewed by an AI voice agent rated it as good as or better than a human.
Greenhouse (mid-Sep): candidates are abandoning AI interviews.

Most people will share whichever one matches their bias. 
I think both are right, and the gap between them is the most 
useful hiring insight I've seen this quarter.

Bullhorn surveyed people placed through staffing agencies. 
They want the contract, fast. They're being processed. 
A bot that picks up at 11pm is a feature.

Direct applicants are doing something else. They're choosing. 
And you can't sell a team, a manager or a mission through a bot.

So this is what I'm taking away:
AI works when the candidate is being processed.
It fails when the candidate is choosing.

Apply that to tech hiring. 

A senior backend engineer in Bengaluru with three offers is always choosing. 
Put an AI screen in front of her and you haven't saved time. You've lost her.

A 2,000-applicant campus drive? Different story.
Same week, SThree grew its contract order book 5% with 7% fewer recruiters. 

Recruiting is being rebuilt the same way engineering is: fewer hands, more leverage.
The recruiters who win won't be the ones who automate the most. 
They'll be the ones who know exactly where not to.

Personally - I am not a fan of AI interviews because recruiting is a "People" business

Engineers: have you ever dropped out of a process because of an AI screen?

Your sales team wins another contract. Delivery asks for another hire.

Before you approve it, ask:

 Are you short of expertise — or is that expertise buried in coordination?

Illustrative desk math:

 12,000 tickets × 10 minutes = 2,000 hours.
 Same volume at 8 minutes = 1,600 hours.
 That’s 400 hours a month released.

Not a headcount cut. Room to grow.

Before your service desk hires again, find the missing 400 hours.
Where those hours actually go in an MSP service desk:
• collecting context the customer already gave
• switching between  PSA-professional service automation, Teams, Chat and email
• chasing approvals
• rewriting the same notes in two systems
• re-explaining the issue after every handoff

Those are skilled people doing glue work. Hiring into that workflow gives you two people doing the same avoidable work.

How Tryvium helps an MSP take those hours back

Tryvium is an Experience Orchestration Platform. It does not replace your PSA or ITSM. It sits on the stack you already run and coordinates AI agents, human expertise, and connected systems so the technician stops being the integration layer.
Concretely, that is how handle time comes down:

Persistent context. Intent, history, and ticket state travel with the interaction. Customers and employees stop repeating themselves. Agents stop rebuilding the story.

Intelligent flow, not blind escalation. Tryvium decides what AI can complete, what a system can execute, and where a human must approve or intervene. Simple work does not automatically become a queue.

End-to-end execution. Collect the information, check policy, route the approval, update the system of record, close the loop — as one designed workflow, not five manual steps.

Humans on judgment, not logistics. Engineers stay on exceptions, client nuance, and the work that actually needs them.

One place to see what is happening. Real-time visibility across the flow, so you can improve the workflow instead of staffing the bottleneck.

In practice that often looks like: Employee starts in Microsoft Teams, orchestration runs the approved path, ServiceNow (or your ITSM) stays the system of record, and the agent only steps in when judgment is required.

One published employee-support deployment reported 30–35% lower average handle time and 40–42% higher agent productivity. Vendor-reported, one environment. Enough to justify a measured pilot. Not a blanket claim for every MSP queue.

Give the recovered hours a job:

 absorb the new contract · cut overtime · fix account health · or productize workflow orchestration as an MSP offer

Prove one high-volume workflow first. Baseline it. Check integrations and client-data boundaries. Then decide whether to hire, redeploy, or sell it.

An open developer position costs more than recruitment fees.

Imagine a HealthTech team needs one senior backend engineer.

The role stays open for 60 days.

What actually happens during those 60 days?

The work doesn't disappear.

It gets distributed.

A senior engineer takes on extra development.

The Engineering Manager gets pulled deeper into delivery.

A planned integration moves to the next sprint.

Technical debt gets pushed again.
And eventually...
“We're hiring” becomes “We're behind.”

This is why I think time-to-hire is also a product metric.

Especially in HealthTech, where engineering teams may simultaneously be handling:
→ Customer implementations
→ Healthcare integrations
→ Platform modernization
→ Security & compliance requirements
→ Data engineering
→ AI initiatives
→ Existing production systems

Every critical position left open creates pressure somewhere else.

Of course, hiring faster should never mean lowering the bar.

The better goal is:
Reduce the time wasted before the right candidate reaches the interview.
Clearer requirements.
Better technical screening.
Smaller, relevant shortlists.
Realistic notice-period expectations.
And the right mix of permanent and contract hiring when timelines demand it.

Because sometimes the question isn't:
“How much will it cost us to hire this developer?”

It's:
“What is it costing us every week that we haven't?”

For HealthTech and Healthcare IT leaders — which technology roles are currently taking the longest for you to close?

Thinking of hiring a company for SEO, AEO & GEO?

Don’t choose one just because they offer the lowest price or promise “#1 rankings.”

Before signing the contract, ask these questions 👇
1️⃣ Do they understand your business?
Your strategy should start with your industry, audience, competitors, services and business goals, not just a list of keywords.
2️⃣ Do they have a proper SEO strategy?
Technical SEO, content, on-page optimisation, internal linking, authority building, local SEO and conversion optimisation all matter.
3️⃣ What exactly are they doing for AEO?
AEO isn't simply adding FAQs to your website. It’s about creating content that clearly answers the questions your potential customers are asking.
4️⃣ Do they understand GEO & AI Search?
Ask them how they plan to improve your visibility across AI-driven search experiences such as ChatGPT, Gemini and other platforms.
And be careful of anyone promising “guaranteed ChatGPT rankings.”
5️⃣ How will they measure results?
Don't settle for a monthly keyword report.
Look at:
-Search visibility
- Organic traffic
-AI/answer visibility
- Brand mentions & citations
- Qualified enquiries
- Conversions
- ROI

6️⃣ Who is actually working on your account?
SEO isn't performed by a single magic tool.
Understand the team behind your strategy, SEO specialists, content writers, developers, strategists and other resources required for execution.
7️⃣ Can they show real case studies?
Don't just ask for screenshots of keywords ranking #1.
Ask:
- Where did the client start?
- What was done?
- What changed?
And what business impact did it create?

8️⃣ Do they understand your business ROI?
Because ultimately:
- Ranking is not the goal.
- Visibility is not the goal.
- Traffic is not the goal.
- The real goal is business growth.

So before you compare agencies based on ₹10K vs ₹50K vs ₹1L per month, compare the strategy, team, execution, scope and expected business outcome.

The cheapest SEO company isn't necessarily expensive.
And the most expensive one isn't necessarily the best.

The right question is:
“What am I actually getting for what I'm paying?”

Interviewer asked me "How can we conduct contract testing using Playwright?" 

First correction I had to do: We cannot conduct contract testing as it natively cannot hold "consumer" & "provider" contracts. But we can explore "json-schema" validations. Which is the next best!

To understand json-schema validation we need 4 steps: 
1) Access to API spec (API Contract)
2) Create Json Schema (generate json schema using: )
3) Store json schema in your framework 
4) Use AJV/ZOD to compile schema and validate with response/request body used/received after execution of API test.

Always remember: JSON Schema validation is one technique used inside contract testing. It is not a synonym for contract testing itself.

What it covers: field presence, data types, required versus optional fields, string formats, nested structure. All of this is expressed once, declaratively, in a schema file.

What it cannot do: 

1) It cannot verify the HTTP status code or response headers were correct.
 
2) It cannot check semantic or business rules a type system cannot express, for example that end_date comes after start_date, or that a total matches the sum of line items.
 
3) It cannot tell you whether the schema reflects a real, agreed contract, or just whatever the API happened to return the one time it was sampled.

Quick tip: If you review the API spec carefully after every change made by Backend teams. Then we can use: "toJsonSchema" to dynamically generate schema using a flag. 
If set to true, it updates the schema files and we just validate the final playwright report.

Ema does not charge per seat or per token. It gets paid when the task is finished.

The company runs teams of AI agents across HR, IT and finance work, and this week raised $77 million in a Series B led by Creaegis, TechCrunch reported. Its customers include Google, Microsoft, PwC and KPMG. According to TechCrunch, Ema ties its pricing to completed tasks and business outcomes rather than seats or tokens.

The billing model decides who carries the risk when an agent fails.

Under a seat licence, you pay whether anyone uses the tool or not. Under token pricing, you pay for every attempt, including the ones that go nowhere. Either way the vendor is paid for access, and the failed run is your cost.

Pay per finished task and that cost goes back to the vendor. The agent that stalls halfway through a workflow becomes their problem.

Ema says more than 90% of its customers have expanded beyond their first use case, and that revenue has grown 50-fold in two years. It does not say how much of that is down to the pricing.

The model will not suit every job. Someone has to agree in advance what "finished" means, and that definition is where these contracts get argued over.

It still gives any business a sharper question for the next vendor quoting on AI work: when the task does not complete, who pays for it?

Ask us too. A vendor worth hiring will have the answer ready.
